steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on data-efficient contrastive self-supervised learning: which training examples contribute most to contrastive SSL, how that relates to supervised learning, and our subset selection method SAS with its main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Which data points are essential for learning; data selection for supervised learning and SSL
- Why finding important examples for SSL is hard
- Our theory: examples that contribute most to contrastive learning
- Contrast with supervised learning
- Method SAS and experimental results

steps.name: detailed_outline

- Our theory (contrastive SSL)

  - pull groups in a class together -> contrastive loss maximally pushes away other classes
  - (1) high alignment of augmented views within each class, (2) preserve centers of class representations of full-data contrastive learning
  - -> generalization guarantee for linear classifier on representations from subset

  - surprisingly: most for contrastive = least for supervised
  - difficulty: prediction confidence and forgetting score (cite) (times misclassified after being correctly classified)
  - most for contrastive = easy examples, high confidence, low forgetting score; can be dropped from supervised training without harming accuracy (cite)
  - difficult examples (most for supervised) can significantly hurt contrastive learning
- SAS and experiments
  - SAS: Subsets that maximize Augmentation Similarity to full data; various datasets and contrastive methods
  - CIFAR10, CIFAR100 (cite), STL10 (cite), TinyImageNet (cite) (cite); ResNet50 with SimCLR
  - up to 20% of CIFAR100, 40% of STL10 and TinyImageNet excluded without harming downstream performance
  - BYOL: discard 20% of STL10 -> even 2% better than full data
  - SAS subsets beat random by over 3% across datasets and methods incl. SimSiam (cite), MoCo (cite), BYOL (cite)
  - subsets extracted efficiently early in training or with smaller proxy model

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Modern machine learning models are powered by large datasets. But a key question is which data points are essential for learning, and whether more data will always give better performance. Answering this is important because it can reduce the large costs of training on large datasets, improve the performance of the trained models and guide data collection. Because of this, there has been a body of recent research on finding the most essential subsets for supervised learning. But as datasets grow larger, getting high-quality labels for them becomes prohibitively expensive. So there has been a surge in self-supervised (SSL) pretraining on large unlabeled datasets. However, finding the most important data points for SSL is still an open question.

It is actually very challenging to find the examples that contribute the most to SSL. When we have labels, the value of each example for learning can be quantified by its loss (or the confidence of the prediction) or by its gradient norm. The examples that are difficult to learn, i.e. those with a high loss or a large gradient norm during training, are the ones that contribute the most to minimizing the training loss. But without labels, SSL methods cluster examples based on how similar they are to the other data points. So the SSL loss and gradient of each example is tightly coupled with those of the other examples in the dataset, and dropping one example affects the loss and gradient of all the other examples. This makes data selection more challenging for SSL than for supervised learning.

In this work we address this challenge for the first time and find the examples that provably contribute the most to SSL. We focus on contrastive SSL, which learns representations by maximizing the alignment between augmented views of the same examples and minimizing the similarity between augmented views of different examples. We prove that the examples that contribute the most to contrastive learning are the ones with the highest expected similarity between their augmented views and the augmented views of the other examples in their latent class. These examples pull different groups of examples in a class together, which lets the contrastive loss push away the representations of examples in different classes as much as possible. We show that these examples (1) ensure a high alignment between the augmented views of examples in each class, and (2) preserve the centers of the class representations that contrastive learning learns on the full data. Using these properties we give a generalization guarantee for a linear classifier that is trained on the representations we get by applying contrastive learning to the subset.

We observe, maybe surprisingly, that the examples that contribute the most to contrastive learning contribute the least to supervised learning. We measure how difficult examples are for supervised learning using the confidence of the predictions and also the forgetting score, i.e. the number of times an example is misclassified after it was correctly classified during training. We show that the examples that contribute the most to contrastive learning are the easy examples, with high confidence and a low forgetting score for supervised learning. These examples can be safely left out of a supervised learning pipeline without hurting the accuracy. On the other hand, the difficult-to-learn examples that contribute the most to supervised learning can hurt contrastive learning performance significantly.

We evaluate our method extensively on different datasets and with different contrastive learning methods. Our method is called SAS, because it selects Subsets that maximize Augmentation Similarity to the full data. First we apply SAS to CIFAR10, CIFAR100, STL10 and TinyImageNet, with ResNet50 using SimCLR. We show that with SAS, up to 20% of the examples from CIFAR100 and 40% from STL10 and TinyImageNet can be safely excluded without hurting the downstream performance. In the same way, for BYOL, using SAS to discard 20% of the examples from STL10 can even beat the downstream performance of the full data by 2%. In general SAS subsets do better than random subsets by over 3% across these datasets and methods, including SimSiam, MoCo and BYOL. We also show that the subsets that contribute the most to SSL can be extracted efficiently early in training or by using a smaller proxy model.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large datasets power modern machine learning models. However, a key question is: which data points are essential for learning, and will more data always yield better performance? Answering this question is crucial, as it can reduce the substantial costs of training on large datasets, boost the performance of trained models and guide data collection. This has motivated a body of recent research on finding the most essential subsets for supervised learning [1,2,3,4,5,6]. However, as datasets grow larger, obtaining high-quality labels for them becomes prohibitively expensive. As a result, there has been a surge in self-supervised (SSL) pretraining on large unlabeled datasets [7,8,9,10]. Nevertheless, finding the most important data points for SSL has remained an open question.

Finding the examples that contribute the most to SSL is indeed very challenging. When labels are available, the value of every example for learning can be quantified based on its loss (or the confidence of the prediction) or its gradient norm. Effectively, difficult-to-learn examples, i.e. those with high loss or large gradient norm during training, are the ones that contribute the most to minimizing the training loss. In the absence of labels, however, SSL methods cluster examples based on their similarity to the other data points. Therefore, the SSL loss and gradient of every example are tightly coupled with those of the other examples in the dataset, and dropping an example affects the loss and gradient of all the others. This makes data selection inherently more challenging for SSL than for supervised learning.

In this work, we address the above challenge for the first time and find examples that provably contribute the most to SSL. In particular, we focus on contrastive SSL, which learns representations by maximizing the alignment between augmented views of the same examples and minimizing the similarity between augmented views of different examples [7,10,11]. We prove that the examples that contribute the most to contrastive learning are those with the highest expected similarity between their augmented views and the augmented views of other examples in their latent class. Effectively, such examples pull different groups of examples in a class together and enable the contrastive loss to maximally push away representations of examples in different classes. We show that such examples (1) ensure a high alignment between augmented views of examples in every class, and (2) preserve the centers of class representations learned by contrastive learning on the full data. We leverage these properties to provide a generalization guarantee for a linear classifier trained on the representations obtained by applying contrastive learning to the subset.

Perhaps surprisingly, we observe that examples that contribute the most to contrastive learning contribute the least to supervised learning. We quantify the difficulty of examples for supervised learning using the confidence of the predictions as well as the forgetting score [1], i.e. the number of times an example is misclassified after being correctly classified during training. We show that the examples contributing the most to contrastive learning are the easy examples, with high confidence and low forgetting score for supervised learning. Such examples can be safely excluded from a supervised learning pipeline without harming the accuracy [1]. In contrast, difficult-to-learn examples that contribute the most to supervised learning can significantly hurt contrastive learning performance.

We extensively evaluate the performance of our method, SAS, which selects Subsets that maximize Augmentation Similarity to the full data, on various datasets and with different contrastive learning methods. We first apply SAS to CIFAR10, CIFAR100 [12], STL10 [13] and TinyImageNet [14], with ResNet50 using SimCLR [7]. We show that with SAS, up to 20% of examples from CIFAR100 and 40% from STL10 and TinyImageNet [15] can be safely excluded without harming the downstream performance. Similarly, for BYOL, using SAS to discard 20% of examples from STL10 can even outperform the downstream performance of the full data by 2%. In general, SAS subsets outperform random subsets by over 3% across these datasets and methods, including SimSiam [9], MoCo [16] and BYOL [8]. We also demonstrate that the subsets that contribute the most to SSL can be extracted efficiently early in training or using a smaller proxy model.
